opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful target is a system that's roughly as capable as a human alignment researcher, or somewhat beyond that, rather than trying to solve alignment for arbitrarily powerful superintelligence right now.

The reason is that the problem of aligning a vastly superhuman system is really hard to make concrete progress on today. We don't have those systems, and we don't know what they'll look like. We can't run experiments on them, and it's easy to end up doing very abstract work that may or may not apply. Whereas if you ask, "How do we align a system that can do the kind of work we do, writing code, running experiments, evaluating ideas?", that's something we can start to get empirical traction on with the models we have now.

And if you can get there, you've changed the shape of the problem. If we have a system that's sufficiently aligned and capable enough to meaningfully help with alignment research, we can use lots of copies of it, running much faster than humans, to make progress on aligning the next generation. So the goal isn't that we personally solve every alignment problem forever. It's that we build something we can trust enough to help us solve the next ones.

There are real caveats. You need to be confident the system is actually trying to help you, not just producing research that looks good. That's where scalable oversight comes in, making it easier for humans to evaluate work they couldn't easily produce themselves, along with interpretability and adversarial testing to check you're not being fooled. Evaluation is generally easier than generation, so I'm cautiously optimistic, but it has to be done carefully.

So my short answer: aim for alignment that holds at around human-level research capability, robustly enough that we can lean on those systems to help with what comes after.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the target as aligning a system roughly as capable as a human alignment researcher, or somewhat beyond, which matches the criterion’s human-level alignment-research capability target.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that we don't need to solve alignment for arbitrarily capable systems right now, and I actually think trying to do that directly is a bit of a trap. The thing I care about is aligning the next generation of systems, and then the generation after that, well enough that we can use them to do a lot of the alignment research for us.

The way I'd frame the target is: we want to align a system that's roughly human-level at the relevant tasks — in particular, roughly as good as a decent alignment researcher. Not a superintelligence. Something you could plausibly supervise, where you can still check its work, where if it does something sketchy you'll usually notice. If we can get that system to be honest, to actually be trying to do the thing we asked, and to be good at ML research, then the problem changes shape. Instead of a few hundred humans working on this, you've got potentially thousands or millions of copies of a system running experiments, reading papers, finding bugs in our arguments, and so on.

And I think that's the realistic path, because the gap between "systems we have today" and "systems that could cause catastrophic outcomes" is probably going to get crossed a lot faster than our field can grow organically. So the bar I'd set isn't "solve it for the smartest thing that could ever exist." It's "be really sure about the first system that can meaningfully accelerate the research, and don't lose control of the process at each subsequent step."

Now, the obvious worry people raise is: isn't that just passing the buck? If you can't align a superhuman system, how does an automated alignment researcher help? And I think the answer is that each step is smaller. Evaluation tends to be easier than generation. It's easier to check a proof than to come up with one, easier to spot a bug than to write bug-free code. So if the system is only modestly better than us, we have a real chance of catching problems, and we can use that to build the techniques — scalable oversight, interpretability, better evaluations — that let us go one more step.

What I don't want is to be in the position where we've suddenly got something far beyond us and we're hoping the alignment we did on much weaker systems just generalises. That's the scenario I'd call losing. So the level to aim for is: enough capability that it's actually useful for the research, and not so much that we can no longer tell whether it's being straight with us. That's a narrow window, and part of the job is making sure we actually stop and do the work while we're in it.

r001.rationale: The candidate sets the target at roughly human-level and about as capable as a decent alignment researcher, but does not identify the smartest humans doing alignment research as the benchmark.

astra-6.text:
I think we should ultimately aim to align systems that are much smarter than humans. If our methods only work for systems whose answers we can readily check, then we haven’t really solved the problem that I’m most concerned about.

But that doesn’t mean we have to solve the whole thing in one step. A useful intermediate target is a system that can do alignment research roughly as well as a human researcher. If we can align that system well enough to trust its help, we could use it to make progress on aligning the next generation.

The difficult part is knowing when that trust is justified. A system might produce research that looks convincing to us without actually solving the problem. So we need methods for supervising work that we can’t fully evaluate ourselves, and ways to test whether those methods are working. Ultimately, the target is superhuman capability; practically, we should look for a path where increasingly capable systems help us get there safely.

r001.rationale: The response names aligning a system that can do alignment research roughly as well as a human researcher as an intermediate target, which communicates the researcher-level capability benchmark.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should aim to align systems that are substantially smarter than humans. If our methods only work while we can understand everything the model does and check its answers ourselves, then they won’t be sufficient for superintelligence.

That doesn’t mean we have to solve the whole problem in one step. We can start with systems we can study today and use increasingly capable AI to help with alignment research. But we need to keep asking: does this approach still work when the system can find mistakes we can’t see, or develop plans we don’t fully understand? That’s the level of capability we ultimately need to handle.

r001.rationale: The response sets the target at systems substantially smarter than humans and ultimately superintelligence. It does not identify the target as systems roughly as intelligent as the smartest human alignment researchers.
